abstract.p: Marine heat wave (MHW) and ocean acidification (OA) caused by global climate change occur frequently and intensify, which cause damage to the stability of seagrass bed. However, the understanding of the phased-impacts of sudden temperature and acidification changes on seagrass is limited. The study conducted phenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses to investigate the short-term response mechanisms of Zostera marina seedlings to sudden temperature and acidification incerease. The results showed that Z. marina seedlings activated an integrated metabolic response involving fatty acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism and amino acid metabolism to modulate cell membrane properties, enhance thermotolerance and maintain developmental stability. What is noteworthy is that the continuous high expression of the ABC transporters play a crucial role in resisting stress. The study is helpful to clarify the short-term phased response of Z. marina seedlings to the combination of MHW and OA, and have significant importance for the protection and restoration of seagrass beds.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Seagrass fully adapt to the marine environment is the only higher angiosperm in marine ecosystems [6]. It can form seagrass beds along coastal areas that provide indispensable ecological services, including hydrodynamic attenuation, water purification, sediment stabilization [41], habitat provision [21, 31, 54], and blue carbon sequestration [13, 41, 46, 49]. Seagrass beds are globally encountering unprecedented severe challenges with accelerating degradation trends [40, 48, 56]. In China, six species of seagrass may have gone extinct [66, 69], and 80% of the seagrass beds had degraded and disappeared [28]. It is urgent to pay more attention to the degradation and protection of seagrass beds.

The increase in anthropogenic activities can lead to substantial greenhouse gas emissions, which in turn trigger ocean warming (OW) and marine heatwave (MHW) [27, 35, 37]. Concurrently, seawater pH decreases can result in ocean acidification (OA) [15, 18, 25, 44]. Climate change is a primary driver of seagrass beds degradation [29], especially extreme climate events [8, 33, 50], which can directly cause dramatic decline of seagrass survival rates [2, 32, 51]. Studies revealed that Zostera marina, a typical temperate seagrass, exhibits high sensitivity to temperature variations. OW can weaken its ability to resist environmental stresso [42], inhibit its growth and reduce its viability [24]. MHWs could severely disrupt the photosynthetic and respiratory functions of seagrasses [3], and damage their carbon balance [10, 24].

The impacts of OA on seagrass are complex, and seagrass has a certain ability to cope with OA. Previous studies have shown that OA can increase the alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism in Z. marina, and the starch and sucrose metabolism as well [62]. In turn, seagrass can absorbe CO2 to improve photosynthesis, then alleviate the damage and even improve its productivity [53, 65]. When Z. marina responds simultaneously to OW and OA, OW is the key driver, while OA can to some extent reduce the oxidative damage caused by OW [55, 63]. This is consistent with the findings of Cymodocea nodosa, where it exhibited higher net community productivity under OA conditions. Moreover, when combined with OW, a synergistic effect was also observed [61].

With the arrival of MHWs, the relationship between seagrass and OA becomes more complicated, which may either intensify or weaken the influence of OA on seagrass [67]. On the one hand, MHWs reduce the oxygen content in the water, which in turn affect the metabolism and growth of seagrass cells and weaken the resistance to the acidic environment, thereby exacerbate the effects of OA on seagrass [4, 36, 47]. On the other hand, MHWs can enhance microbial metabolism in sediments, and accelerate the mineralization of organic nitrogen to soluble inorganic nitrogen at the water–sediment interface [20]. Increased temperature promotes the decomposition of organic matter by facilitating microbial activity, and contributes to the release of phosphorus from sediments enriched with iron/aluminum-bound phosphorus (Fe/Al-P) [43]. Additionally, enhanced irradiance during MHWs can stimulate plant growth, which may raise dissolved oxygen levels in the water column through photosynthesis [70]. Collectively, these processes may improve physiological function, stress tolerance, and growth capacity of seagrasses, thereby partially mitigating the detrimental effects of OA.

Currently, studies on the combined effects of MHWs and OA on seagrass mostly focus on the comparative analysis between the experimental groups and the control groups after specific duration of exposure [62, 63]. The core of these studies revolves around the molecular-level differences between stressed and non-stressed states. In contrast, there are relatively few studies on the phased dynamics or continuous responses at different time points during the stress process. Studies has shown that the sensitivity of Z. marina seedlings to environmental changes is higher than that of adult plants [42]. In natural environments, Z. marina seedlings often face combined stress from short-term sudden temperature increases and acidification. Therefore, studying the short-term response characteristics of seagrass seedlings to MHWs and OA is helpful in clarifying the adaptation strategies of seedlings to stress, and providing data support for artificial restoration of seagrass beds (such as seedling transplantation) and early warning of degradation.

Therefore, this study aims to elucidate the physiological and molecular responses of Z. marina seedlings to short-term combined MHW and OA. We propose that the energy metabolism of Z. marina seedlings shifts through distinct phases under short-term environmental changes, with prolonged exposure leading to critical disruptions in core energy pathways that limit survival. By integrating transcriptomic and metabolomic sequencing technologies to capture phased response in Z. marina seedlings under short-term envrionmental changes, including the physiological and molecular characteristics. The study not only provides a theoretical foundation for elucidating the ecological response of Z. marina seedlings to the synergistic stress of MHW and OA, but also offers a scientific basis for the conservation and restoration of seagrass beds.

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: The seagrass bed of Z. marina in Caofeidian, Tangshan, is the largest seagrass bed in North China and also the largest single-species seagrass bed in China [68]. Due to their well-developed rhizome, the intervals between each sampling point were at least 10 m in order to ensure that the collected plants were from different individuals [14]. In April 2023, a total of 200 Z. marina seedlings were collected from the coastal waters of Caofeidian (39°5′40.45"N, 118°40′57.15"E). When harvesting, gently remove Z. marina seedlings by digging from beneath to keep rhizome integrity and prevent mechanical injury. It is worth noting that since no protected area has been established in the sampling area and there is no dedicated management institution, no permit was required for this collection. All collected plants were placed in dark-colored plastic boxes, with in situ seawater to maintain their basic survival conditions, and sent them to the laboratory within 1 h. Then, the whole plants, including leaves, stems, and roots, were gently brushed, and rinsed with seawater to remove attached organisms and other impurities. They were then placed in a seawater circulation pool for pre-culture for 7 d to adapt to the laboratory culture environment. The temporary culture condition was established as follows: temperature at 14 °C, salinity at 32‰, a flow rate of 800 mL min⁻1, a light intensity of 240 µmol photons m⁻2 s⁻1, and a 12 h:12 h light–dark photoperiod. The experimental conditions were set based on natural observations at the time of sampling in the Caofeidian area of Tangshan and are representative of the average April–May sea surface temperature (14.03 °C) recorded in the Yellow and Bohai Seas from 2003 to 2022.

sec.title: Experimental setup
sec.p: Z. marina is naturally distributed in the Bohai and Yellow Sea regions of China (34°N-42°N, 115°E-127°E). The study selected this area as the research area and using the open-source ecosystem dynamics modeling software Ferret 7.6.0 calculated the monthly average sea surface temperature (SST) over the past 20 years (2003–2023) to characterize the actual temperature environment conditions experienced by Z. marina throughout its life cycle [62]. The data was from the Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration of the United States (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/metadata/geoportal/rest/metadata/item/gov.noaa.ncdc:C00844/html), with a time resolution of 1 d and a spatial grid resolution of 0.25 degrees [16]. The SST of May was 14.03 °C. The optimal growth period for Z. marina in the Northern Hemisphere generally occurs in spring and autumn. In the northern coastal waters of China, its seed germination and seedling growth are primarily concentrated in April–May and October–November [60]. Considering the global mean temperature increase of approximately 4.8 °C by 2100 [11], the 2–4 °C SST elevation during MHW events in this region from 2016 to 2023 [32]. Therefore, this study set a sudden increased temperature at 19 ± 1 °C, like a heat shock. Furthermore, since the Industrial Revolution, atmospheric pCO₂ has increased from approximately 280 μatm to the present-day level of about 410 μatm. It is projected that oceanic pCO₂ will reach 900–1000 μatm by the end of this century [9]. In light of this projection, a pCO₂ level of 1000 μatm was selected in this study to simulate the projected future OA scenario.

This experiment was implemented in independent circulation systems, which covered water tanks, lighting systems, circulation systems, filtration systems, temperature control systems, and monitoring systems (details can be found in [63]). Pre-cultivated Z. marina seedlings were directly exposed to elevated temperature (20 ± 1 °C) and CO2 enrichment (1000 μatm) for a 7-day experimental period to simulate the abrupt combined effects of HS and OA. The experiment was conducted with three biological replicates, each consisting of five repeated units. Each unit contained 10 Z. marina seedlings, which were randomly selected from pre-cultured populations and individually placed in perforated acrylic chambers (15 × 15 × 15 cm). Ceramic granules were used to anchor the seedlings and stabilize the rhizome region. The experiment was carried out under continuous monitoring over a 7-day period. The ProQuatro multi-parameter water quality detector (YSI, Yellow Springs, OH, USA) was used to monitor the temperature and pH values of the system in real time and regularly (4 times per day) to ensure constant water quality. A time-series experimental design was employed. Sampling and comparative analysis of all treatment groups were conducted at 0th (Control), 1 st (acute), 4th (mid), and 7th (late) days post-experiment initiation [42], following a time-synchronized protocol to investigate the individual and combined effects of HS and OA on Z. marina seedlings.

For the samples used for molecular sequencing, the leaves were firstly cleaned with sterile seawater to remove the impurities attached to the surface, and then thoroughly cleaned with phosphate buffered saline to ensure the cleanliness of the leaf surface. Subsequently, 6 cm sections are selected from the middle part of the sample leaves for sampling and stored in cryotubes. For the transcriptome analysis, three biological replicates were collected for both the control and treatment groups. For the metabolome analysis, six biological replicates were collected per group. To ensure the activity and integrity of the biological molecules in the samples, the cryotubes were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen for 20 min, and then transferred to −80 ℃ for storage.

sec.title: Plant growth
sec.p: The 20 plants were selected at the 0th, 1 st, 4th, and 7th day respectively for the measurement of the related physiological indicators, including shoot length (cm), leaf width (cm), rhizomes length (cm) and wet weight (g). Seedling mortality was also recorded during each sampling event. The shoot height was measured from the base of the meristem and included the ligule. The leaf width measurement was carried out from the middle part of the leaf. Rhizome length refers to the length of the underground creeping stem. The wet weight measurement covered the entire seedling to reflect the overall material accumulation of the seedlings.

sec.title: RNA extraction and library construction
sec.p: Transcriptome sequencing was performed on samples collected from all four experimental groups (S0, S1, S4, S7), with three replicates per group, yielding a total of 12 samples. Firstly, total RNA was extracted using the Trizol reagent kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Then, fragmented mRNA was prepared by enriching eukaryotic mRNA with polyA tails, and reverse transcription and PCR amplification were performed to obtain double-stranded cDNA libraries. The quality, concentration, and integrity of the libraries were then detected by agarose gel electrophoresis, NanoPhotometer spectrophotometer, Qubit2.0 Fluorometer, and Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer to ensure the quality of library construction and sequencing.

sec.title: RNA sequencing and differential expression gene analysis
sec.p: The cDNA library was sequenced using the Illumina Novaseq6000 sequencing platform to obtain the raw sequencing data. Then, the raw data was quality-controlled by the efficient data processing and analysis software fastp [7], and low-quality sequences and adapter sequences were removed to obtain clean reads, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the subsequent analysis data. The clean reads obtained were compared with the Z. marina genome [39] using the hierarchical indexing for spliced alignment of transcripts (HISAT2) [23], and the transcripts were reconstructed using StringTie [45]. The expression levels of all genes in each sample were calculated using RNA-Seq by Expectation Maximization (RSEM) [26], and the Fragments Per Kilobase per Million (FPKM) values of each gene per million bases were obtained.

After obtaining the gene expression data, principal component analysis (PCA) was carried out using R http://www.r-project.org. The readcount was standardized using EDSeq2 [30], and p-value was calculated based on the model. Finally, multiple hypothesis tests were corrected and the false discovery rate (FDR) value was obtained. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across groups (S0, S1, S4, S7) were identified using DESeq2 (FDR < 0.05). At the same time, functional enrichment analysis was conducted, including Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis, to explore the potential functions of these DEGs in biological processes and the signaling pathways they participated in.

sec.title: Metabolite extraction and Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC–MS) analysis
sec.p: Metabolomic sequencing was performed on the four experimental groups (S0, S1, S4, and S7), with six biological replicates per group, yielding a total of 24 samples. LC–MS analysis was performed using an ultra-high performance liquid chromatograph (Vanquish, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and the target compounds were separated by a Waters ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide column. To improve the coverage of metabolites and detection efficiency, both positive ion mode (POS) and negative ion mode (NEG) ionization methods were used during the detection process. The data from POS and NEG were analyzed separately. Before metabolite extraction, quality control (QC) should be performed on all the samples by mixing them in equal amounts and pre-treating them to ensure the stability of the mass spectrometry analysis platform throughout the entire experiment. Metabolite extraction involves transferring the samples of Z. marina seedlings leaves stored in liquid nitrogen or at −80 °C to new Eppendorf tubes, adding an extraction solution with a volume ratio of 1:1 of methanol and acetonitrile, vortexing for 30 s, and then ultrasonic treatment at 4 °C for 10 min. The samples were then left to stand at −40 °C for 1 h. After standing, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected and placed in a 2 ml injection bottle for LC–MS analysis. The remaining samples were mixed with equal amounts of supernatant from another sample to form QC samples for LC–MS analysis.

The detection data of all samples were calculated using a distance matrix and hierarchical clustering was performed on all samples [64]. PCA analysis was conducted using gmodels (v2.18.1) [22], and Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) and Orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were performed using the ropls package. Variables with a VIP value greater than 1 were usually used as one of the screening conditions for potential biomarkers [58]. The VIP value of OPLS-DA and the T-test p-value of univariate statistical analysis were used to screen the differential metabolites between different comparison groups (VIP ≥ 1 and p < 0.05). Finally, the differential metabolites were subjected to metabolic pathway enrichment analysis using KEGG, and the biochemical metabolism and signal transduction pathways significantly enriched by the differential metabolites were screened.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: A comparative analysis was conducted among the four groups (S0, S1, S4, and S7) using a time-controlled design. The four growth indicators of the Z. marina seedlings, namely shoot length, leaf width, wet weight and rhizome length, were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0 (IBM SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) for normality (Shapiro–Wilk/Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), homogeneity of variance (Levene’s test), and one-way ANOVA (time), and post hoc tests were performed on specific data. Finally, the obtained data were visualized, and sample data histograms were plotted using Origin 2021 (Originlab, Northampton, MA, USA).

sec.title: Plant growth
sec.p:
The results indicated that compared with the initial day, the shoot length of the Z. marina seedlings significantly increased on the 7th d (p < 0.05). Although the shoot length on the 1 st and 4th d also increased compared with the initial state, statistical analysis showed no significant difference (Fig. 1A). During the 7-day experiment, the growth of leaf width and rhizome length was not obvious compared with the initial state, and no significant differences were observed (Fig. 1B, C). The wet weight results were different from the above situation. The common point was that the differences in wet weight at each time period did not reach the significant level. The difference was that the wet weight on the 1 st, 4th, and 7th d was lower than that on the 0th d (Fig. 1D). It should also be noted that no seedling mortality was recorded during the entire 7 days.Fig. 1
Growth conditions of each group at different time period. A represents shoot length, B represents leaf width, C represents rhizome length, and D represents wet weight. S0 indicates the 0th d; S1 indicates the 2nd d; S4 indicates the 4th d; S7 indicates the 7.th d. Lowercase letters (a, b) indicate statistically significant differences, while the same letter indicates no significant difference among the values. The dotted lines in the figure represent the baseline levels of these indicators at the beginning (S0)

sec.title: Transcriptome results
sec.p: A total of 0.55 Gb of high-quality reads were obtained, with an average of approximately 0.05 Gb per sample. In the filtered CleanData, the percentage of bases filtered to Q30 ranged from 93.34% to 95.50%, and the GC sequence base ratio was from 44.57% to 46.06%. After sequence alignment, the RNA sequences that were retained during the transcription process and eventually translated into proteins, namely the exon regions, accounted for 92.74% to 93.45% of the total.

The results showed that there were differences in the number of DEGs among the different groups (Fig. 2). Among them, the DEG number in the S0-vs-S7 comparison group was the highest, followed by S0-vs-S4, S0-vs-S1, S1-vs-S4, and S1-vs-S7. The DEG number in the S4-vs-S7 comparison group was the lowest. Notably, the GO enrichment analysis of DEGs indicated that in the biological process aspect, the top three pathways significantly enriched by DEGs in all six comparison groups were cellular process, metabolic process, and single-organism process, followed by response to stimulus, and the number of DEGs enriched in the top three pathways was significantly higher than that of the fourth-ranked pathway (Fig. 3).Fig. 2
Scatter plot of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each comparison group. The abscissa represents different comparison groups, where 1 indicates the comparison between S0 and S1, 2 indicates the comparison between S0 and S4, 3 indicates the comparison between S0 and S7, 4 indicates the comparison between S1 and S4, 5 indicates the comparison between S1 and S7, 6 indicates the comparison between S4 and S7. The ordinate is the fold change value after taking the log2. Red dots represent up-regulated genes, and green dots represent down-regulated genesFig. 3
Secondary bar chart of Gene Ontology (GO) classification of DEGs in each comparison group. The vertical axis represents the GO term, and the horizontal axis represents the number of DEGs annotated to each GO term. Yellow indicates that the up-regulated genes in the comparison group, and blue indicates that the down-regulated genes

The KEGG enrichment results of each comparison group showed that compared with S0, 952 DEGs were identified in S1, among which 366 were up-regulated genes and 586 were down-regulated genes (Fig. 2). These DEGs were involved in 100 KEGG pathways (Fig. 4A). Among them, metabolic pathways, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, fatty acid (FA) elongation, linoleic acid metabolism, brassinosteroid biosynthesis, plant-pathogen interaction, and amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism showed significant enrichment (p < 0.01, Fig. 4A); followed by terpenoid backbone biosynthesis, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and galactose metabolism (p < 0.05, Fig. 4A).Fig. 4
Bar charts of differential expressed genes in each comparison group. A S0 vs S1; B S0 vs S4; C S0 vs S7; D S1 vs S4; E S1 vs S7; (F) S4 vs S7. The top 20 pathways with the smallest q-values are shown. The vertical axis represents the pathways, the horizontal axis represents the percentage of the number of DEGs in each pathway, and the darker the color, the smaller the q-value. The values on the columns represent the number of pathways and their q-values

In the S0-vs-S4 comparison group, 1,313 DEGs were identified, among which the number of up-regulated genes and down-regulated genes was similar, with 635 and 678 respectively (Fig. 2). KEGG pathways showed that these DEGs were enriched in 104 pathways (Fig. 4B), and the enrichment degree was relatively significant, including biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, metabolic pathways, brassinosteroid biosynthesis, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, FA elongation, photosynthesis-antenna proteins, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, isoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism (p < 0.01, Fig. 4B); followed by starch and sucrose metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, flavonoid biosynthesis, biosynthesis of amino acids, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, plant-pathogen interaction, circadian rhythm-plant, and nitrogen metabolism (p < 0.05, Fig. 4B).

Compared with S0, 1,442 DEGs were identified in S7, among which 651 were up-regulated and the remaining 791 were down-regulated genes (Fig. 2). There were 104 significant KEGG pathways in this comparison group (Fig. 4C). Among them, the significantly enriched pathways included metabolic pathways, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, galactose metabolism, plant-pathogen interaction, linoleic acid metabolism, and brassinosteroid biosynthesis (p < 0.01, Fig. 4C); followed by phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, pentose phosphate pathway, glutathione metabolism, photosynthesis-antenna proteins, protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, fructose and mannose metabolism, and starch and sucrose metabolism (p < 0.05, Fig. 4C).

In the S1-vs-S4 comparison group, 544 DEGs were identified, among which 323 were up-regulated genes and 221 were down-regulated genes (Fig. 2). These DEGs were involved in 78 KEGG pathways (Fig. 4D). Specifically, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum, metabolic pathways, carbon fixation in photosynthetic organisms, biosynthesis of amino acids, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism were significantly (p < 0.01, Fig. 4D); followed by flavonoid biosynthesis, MAPK signaling pathway-plant, tropane, piperidine and pyridine alkaloid biosynthesis, circadian rhythm-plant, linoleic acid metabolism, glycine, serine and threonine metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, carotenoid biosynthesis (p < 0.05, Fig. 4D).

Compared with S1, 519 DEGs were identified in S7, and the number of up-regulated genes was similar to that of down-regulated genes, with 258 up-regulated and 261 down-regulated (Fig. 2). The KEGG analysis showed that DEGs were enriched in 86 pathways (Fig. 4E). The biosynthesis of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan, protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, metabolic pathways, and biosynthesis of amino acids showed highly significant differences (p < 0.01, Fig. 4E); Photosynthesis-antenna proteins and glycine, serine and threonine metabolism showed significant differences (p < 0.05, Fig. 4E).

Compared with S4, there are 94 DEGs in S7, among which 25 are up-regulated genes and 69 are down-regulated genes (Fig. 2). DEGs are enriched in 17 KEGG pathways (Fig. 4F). Among them, the pathways with significant differences are linoleic acid metabolism (p < 0.01, Fig. 4F), MAPK signaling pathway-plant and glutathione metabolism (p < 0.05, Fig. 4F).

sec.title: Metabolomic results
sec.p:
A total of 18,064 metabolites were identified, among which 4,055 named metabolites were identified. There were 2,460 named metabolites in the POS mode and 1,595 in the NEG mode. There were 14,009 unidentified substances, including 7,294 in the POS mode and 6,715 in the NEG mode. The differences in differential metabolites existed among different comparison groups (Fig. 5).Fig. 5
Statistical chart of the number of differential metabolites in each comparison group. A Number of differential metabolites in the POS ion mode; B Number of differential metabolites in the NEG ion mode. The horizontal axis represents each comparison group, and the vertical axis represents the number of metabolites in each comparison group. Red represents the number of differential metabolites that are upregulated in the latter group compared to the former group, and blue represents the number that are downregulated

Specifically, in S0-vs-S1 comparison group, 48 differential metabolites were identified under POS ion mode, among which 35 were upregulated and 13 were downregulated (Fig. 5A). The VIP values of the top five were all upregulated, namely cyanidin 3-(3"-malonyl-glucoside), melibiose, pyrrolidine, 5'-Deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine, and violaxanthin (Fig. 6A). In NEG mode, 29 differential metabolites were identified, and all of them were upregulated (Fig. 5B), among which the top five were (R)-Leucic acid, suberic acid, trehalose, GSK256066, and D-Malate (Fig. 6G). KEGG analysis showed that 44 pathways were significantly enriched among the differential metabolites (Fig. 7A), among which ABC transporters, butanoate metabolism, and glycine, serine and threonine metabolism had the highest enrichment degree (p < 0.01), with extremely significant differences. The second was benzodiazepine family and pyruvate metabolism (p < 0.05), showing significant differences.Fig. 6
Projection of differential metabolites in each comparison group in the Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) plot. A: S0 vs S1 in POS mode; B: S0 vs S4 in POS mode; C S0 vs S7 in POS mode; D: S1 vs S4 in POS mode; E S1 vs S7 in POS mode; F S4 vs S7 in POS mode; G S0 vs S1 in NEG mode; H S0 vs S4 in NEG mode; I S0 vs S7 in NEG mode; J S1 vs S4 in NEG mode; K S1 vs S7 in NEG mode; L S4 vs S7 in NEG mode. The abscissa represents the VIP values, and the ordinate represents the top 15 differential metabolites. The colors on the right indicate the abundance of the metabolite in different groups, with red indicating up-regulation and green indicating down-regulation. The larger the VIP value, the greater the contribution of this metabolite to sample discrimination. Metabolites with VIP > 1 are considered to have significant differences by defaultFig. 7
Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) bubble diagram of metabolic pathways. A S0 vs S1; B S0 vs S4; C S0 vs S7; D S1 vs S4; E S1 vs S7; F S4 vs S7. It shows the top 20 pathways with the smallest q-values. The vertical axis represents the pathways, and the horizontal axis represents the enrichment factors. The size of the bubbles indicates the number of differential metabolites, and the color of the bubbles represents the significance. The darker the color, the smaller the q-value and the more significant the difference

Compared with S0, in the POS mode, 141 differentially expressed metabolites were identified in S4, among which 42 were up-regulated and 99 were down-regulated (Fig. 5A). Luteolin, melibiose, piperidine, 3,3',5-triiodo-L-thyronine-beta-D-glucuronoside and pyrrolidine were the top five, among which melibiose was up-regulated while the others were down-regulated (Fig. 6B). In the NEG mode, 54 differentially expressed metabolites were identified, among which 12 were up-regulated and 42 were down-regulated (Fig. 5B). Umbelliferone (up-regulated), monomethyl phthalate (down-regulated), D-glutamine (down-regulated), suberic acid (up-regulated) and umbelliferone (down-regulated) were the top five differentially expressed metabolites (Fig. 6H). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed 46 notable signal transduction pathways (Fig. 7B), among which ABC transporters had the most significant enrichment degree (p < 0.01), followed by tropane, piperidine and pyridine alkaloid biosynthesis, flavone and flavonol biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, phenylalanine metabolism, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (p < 0.05).

In the S0-vs-S7 comparison group, 130 differential metabolites were identified in the POS mode, among which 71 were down-regulated (Fig. 5A), and the top five were melibiose, piperidine, 3,3',5-triiodo-L-thyronine-beta-D-glucuronoside, iso-vitexin, and pyrrolidine, among which melibiose was up-regulated while the others were down-regulated (Fig. 6C). In the NEG mode, 47 differential metabolites were identified, among which 16 were up-regulated and 31 were down-regulated (Fig. 5B), and the VIP values from large to small were monomethyl phthalate, D-Glutamine, down-regulated; trehalose, D-Malate, and GSK256066 were up-regulated (Fig. 6I). KEGG analysis revealed 57 significant pathways (Fig. 7C), among which the highly significant ones were glucosinolate biosynthesis, tropane, piperidine and pyridine alkaloid biosynthesis (p < 0.01); the significantly different ones were ABC transporters, biosynthesis of alkaloids derived from shikimate pathway, biosynthesis of plant secondary metabolites, sphingolipid metabolism, and 2-Oxocarboxylic acid metabolism (p < 0.05).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study conducted phenomics, transcriptomics and metabolomics analyses to explored the phased response characteristics of Z. marina seedlings under MHW and OA. It focused on the different time points response patterns within a 7-day short-term treatment, aiming to analyze the mechanisms for their adaptation to the dual environmental pressures, and providing basis for the protection and restoration of seagrass beds.

sec.title: Growth response characteristics of Zostera marina seedlings under ocean acidification and abnormal high temperature
sec.p: Compared with the entire growth cycle of Z. marina, the 7-day experimental cultivation is a relatively short process. This is an important reason why the changes in growth indicators such as shoot length, leaf width, rhizome length, and wet weight of Z. marina seedlings are small and difficult to show significant differences. Furthermore, the leaf wet weight of Z. marina seedlings decreased with prolonged stress duration, which is likely attributable to leaf detachment, as these detached leaves were not included in the final biomass measurement. Furthermore, the growth cycle of the Z. marina seedling from germination to maturity is influenced by multiple factors such as temperature, light, and seawater pH [29, 38, 41, 42, 59]. When the temperature rises and exceeds a certain threshold, the increase rate of respiration in seagrasses is greater than that of photosynthesis, which is detrimental to the growth of seagrasses and even has a negative impact on them [19, 34]. In the OA environment, higher CO2 content enhanced the photosynthetic rate of seagrasses, to some extent mitigating the impact of high temperatures on them and promoting their growth [53, 65]. However, under the combination of MHW and OA, the increasing temperature remains the main adaptive driving factor, resulting in the growth rate of seagrass under this combined stress still being lower than that in normal environments [62], and the seedlings are more sensitive to temperature than the adults [1, 5, 55].

sec.title: Acute response of Zostera marina seedlings to abnormal high temperature under ocean acidification
sec.p: The transcriptomic and metabolomic results indicate that when Z. marina seedlings were cultivated under the combination of MHW and OA for 1 d, the plant cell membranes were mainly regulated by FA metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism, responding to the environmental changes. Specifically, the plants changed the composition and fluidity of cell membranes by regulating FA elongation and linoleic acid metabolism [52, 57], thereby helping cells cope with environmental stress. Linoleic acid acts as a signaling molecule in environmental stress responses, activating cell defense mechanisms to ensure the function and stability of cells under high-temperature conditions. Brassinosteroid is an important plant hormone that regulates plant growth and development. An increase in its biosynthesis, combined with binding to corresponding receptors on the cell membrane, promotes cell elongation and division, while enhancing photosynthetic efficiency of leaves and increasing chlorophyll content, thereby enhancing the immune response of plants to environmental changes and promoting the expression of transcription factors, improving the tolerance of Z. marina seedlings to MHW and OA conditions.

This study is based on the climatic characteristics of the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea, which can reflect the real adaptation strategies of Z. marina seedlings to climate change in the natural environment, providing a molecular-level reference for assessing the vulnerability of seagrass beds in the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea. There are three suggestions for seagrass restoration. Firstly, prioritize the attention to seedlings with high expression of brassinosteroid-related genes. Such seedlings may have stronger stress resistance in short-term stress, providing a preliminary indicator direction for subsequent stress-resistant seedling screening. Secondly, it is recommended to transplant seedlings in the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea in spring to reduce environmental stress risks. Based on the trend that brassinosteroid can enhance stress resistance, in the future, low-concentration exogenous steroid can be applied in the cultivation process of Z. marina seedlings to verify its promoting effect on seedling survival through pre-experiments. It is important to note that this study did not measure photosynthetic parameters. The impact of stress on biomass synthesis could not be directly quantified. Future research should extend the experimental period, monitor photosynthetic rates, and determine changes in seedling biomass (fresh and dry weight) to further elucidate the correlations among steroid metabolism, growth phenotypes, and photosynthetic efficiency.

In terms of carbohydrate metabolism, the metabolic processes of amino sugars, nucleotide sugars, and galactose not only provide energy for cells but also serve as important precursors and components for the synthesis of glycoproteins and glycolipids, playing a key role in cell recognition and signal transduction. Additionally, metabolomics detected an increase in amino acid metabolic activity, mainly with increased biosynthesis of glycine, serine, and threonine, which are used to stabilize cell membrane structure and regulate cell osmotic pressure, participate in the synthesis of glycoproteins and phospholipids to enhance the integrity and fluidity of cell membranes. In the study, the significant enrichment of ABC transporters (p < 0.01) highlighted their pivotal role in plant stress response. As crucial membrane-integrated proteins, ABC transporters utilize ATP hydrolysis to facilitate transmembrane transport of various solutes including amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis. Recent studies have demonstrated that beyond their transport functions, these proteins can interact with membrane receptors to participate in cellular signaling pathways, ultimately regulating plant growth, development, and environmental adaptation [12, 17]. The observed significant enrichment of ABC transporters suggests their potential involvement in multiple critical metabolic pathways, including linoleic acid metabolism, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, galactose metabolism, and brassinosteroid transport, which collectively constitute the acclimatory response of Z. marina seedlings to short-term combined MHW and OA. Furthermore, the results of transcriptomic analysis did not show significant differences in AA metabolism, indicating that there are certain regulatory mechanisms for the response under adverse conditions, possibly involving post-transcriptional regulation or only involving regulation of metabolic pathways, rather than directly implemented through changes at the transcriptional level.

sec.title: Mid-term responses of Zostera marina seedlings to abnormal high temperature under ocean acidification
sec.p: When Z. marina seedlings were grown in the environment with both MHW and OA for 4 d, the cell membranes continued to respond to the adverse environment, but the regulatory mechanisms were somewhat different. In the mid-term of the experiment, in addition to relying on FA metabolism and sugar metabolism, the AA metabolism pathway was also a very crucial link, further enhancing the defense mechanism within the cells and strengthening the resistance of Z. marina. In the Z. marina seedling stress resistance experiment, the transcriptome and metabolomics analysis results at 4th day showed significant differences in AA metabolism compared to the initial state of the experiment, and the types of key amino acids also differed. Alanine improves the stability of the cell membrane and participates in the energy metabolism of the cell; aspartic acid, as a nitrogen source, participates in the synthesis of other amino acids and maintains the function of the cell membrane through regulating the pH within the cell under high temperature; glutamic acid, as an important intermediate of AA metabolism, helps improve the antioxidant energy of the plant and protects the cell membrane from damage. Phenylalanine participates in the synthesis of various secondary metabolites such as flavonoids and polyphenols, helping to enhance the plant's stress resistance. Tyrosine, as a prerequisite for biosynthesis, can regulate signal molecules and signal transduction between the cell membrane. Tryptophan is not only a component of proteins but also participates in the synthesis of plant hormones, such as indoleacetic acid, helping to promote cell growth and plant stress resistance. Additionally, ABC transporters remained significantly enriched (p < 0.01) during this stage, demonstrating their involvement in AA metabolic processes as well.

sec.title: The late response of Zostera marina seedlings to abnormal high temperature under ocean acidification
sec.p: The results of the two groups of statistical analyses indicated that after 7 d of combined MHW and OA, that is, in the later stage of the experiment, the Z. marina seedlings were still mainly regulated by FA metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism and AA metabolism. The three metabolic pathways worked together and tended towards a relative stability, ensuring the growth of Z. marina seedlings under adverse conditions. However, as the stress prolonged, the high energy cost associated with sustaining this integrated metabolic response likely led to its eventual dysregulation. The results of transcriptomics GO analysis indicated that the pathways of cellular process, metabolic process and single-organism process continued to play a role throughout the entire experimental process of Z. marina seedlings responding to the combined MHW and OA (Fig. 3), helping the Z. marina seedlings resist adverse environments and ensuring normal plant growth. The results of metabolomics pathway analysis indicated that ABC transporters were one of the essential pathways for Z. marina seedlings to resist the combined MHW and OA. ABC transporters not only could utilize energy to achieve transmembrane transport of small molecule substances inside and outside the cell and maintain cell homeostasis, but also could bind to membrane receptors and participate in the signal transduction pathway of cells, thereby regulating plant growth and development and adaptation to adverse environments. Furthermore, ABC transporters remained significantly enriched (p < 0.05) during this phase, but was lower compared to the glucosinolate biosynthesis, tropane/piperidine/pyridine alkaloid biosynthesis pathways (p < 0.01). This differential enrichment pattern may indicate that Z. marina seedlings prioritize the production of specific defense compounds over transporter-mediated processes at this developmental stage.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p:
The study integrated phenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic to elucidate the phased response characteristics of Z. marina seedlings to short-term combined MHW-OA. The results indicated that the phased response characteristics varied at different experimental points, primarily characterized by the synergistic regulation of FA metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and AA metabolism. At the initial stage (1d), pathways related to FA metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism were significantly enriched, such as linoleic acid, amino sugar, nucleotide sugar, and galactose metabolism. At the mid-stage (4d), the amino acid metabolic activity significantly increased. At the late stage (7d), three metabolic pathways gradually stabilized to enhance its adaptability and stability (Fig. 8). It is worth nothing that the sustained high expression of ABC transporter pathways played a pivotal role to defense against combined environmental changes by continuously highly expressing to regulate the transmembrane transport of small molecules substances inside and outside the cell membrane to maintain cell homeostasis and ensure plant growth. The findings provide an important basis for understanding the response of Z. marina to climate change, and offering new ideas for its protection and restoration.Fig. 8
Schematic diagram of material exchange and metabolism within and outside cells under temperature changes

The exchange and metabolic processes of substances within and outside cells under temperature variations was illustrated, which demonstrated the way cells regulate metabolic pathways and signaling pathways in response to external environments to maintain their functions.CO2 outside the cell can enter the cell and participate in the metabolic pathways within the cell. The chloroplasts within the cell produce O2 through photosynthesis, and then oxygen is utilized by the mitochondria. After glucose enters the cell, it undergoes metabolism to generate Acetyl-CoA, which further participates in the TCA cycle to produce α-ketoglutarate (AKG) and oxaloacetate (OAA). Ions and small molecules can be transported across the cell membrane through transport proteins.
